paragraphs.text: The appellants, XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, his spouse, XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, and their minor children, XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX and XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, citizens of Mexico, are appealing against the decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD), dated August 20, 2019, rejecting their refugee protection claims made under sections 96 and 97 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).
XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX was appointed as the designated representative of the minor children, whose claims are based on his.
The male appellant alleges that he was the victim of assaults and death threats by members of the Jalisco cartel, because he reported them to the police for a crime he had witnessed.

He alleges that, on February 11, 2016, he saw three cartel members named XXXX, XXXX and XXXX remove a person who was covered in blood from their vehicle and put the individual in the trunk. The male appellant called police, who arrested XXXX, one of the members. The same day, he was attacked by XXXX, who threatened to kill him, as well as his family, for reporting them to police. The male appellant made a police complaint so that the events would be investigated.

The next day, XXXX and XXXX went to the male appellant's home and threatened his wife to make them withdraw the complaint or they would regret it. They then broke the windows of their home. On February 15, 2016, the appellants left to seek refuge in a house that belonged to the male appellant's sister-in-law.

On May 9, 2018, while the female appellant was on her way to the pediatrician with the baby, she was accosted by XXXX, who attempted to take the baby from her. She escaped with the help of people on the street who came to her aid.
On May 11, 2018, the male appellant's sister-in-law found the windows of the home where she was housing the appellants broken and a note indicating [translation] "I know where you live."
On May 12, 2018, the appellants sought refuge at the home of the male appellant's grandmother. They then left Mexico on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2018, for Canada, where they claimed refugee protection.
The appellants still fear for their lives should they return to Mexico.

The RPD rejected the appellants' refugee protection claims, concluding that they had an internal flight alternative (IFA) in the towns of Mérida or Campeche. The appellants submit that the RPD erred in assessing their prospective risk in the IFA cities. The appellants are asking the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) to allow the appeal or to order a de novo hearing before another member.

After conducting an independent analysis of all the evidence on the record, including the recording of the hearing, I conclude that the RPD erred in its IFA assessment. Consequently, I set aside the RPD's determination, substitute a determination that, in my opinion, should have been made, and find that the appellants are persons in need of protection under section 97 of the IRPA.

The RAD is required to review the RPD's decision and to conduct its own analysis of all the evidence on the record to determine, in light of the arguments put forward by the appellant, whether the RPD erred. The applicable standard of review in this case is correctness.1 ANALYSIS Credibility

paragraphs.text: Credibility is not at issue, given that the RPD found the appellants to be credible. I am of the opinion that the RPD did not err in this regard. Internal flight alternative in Mexico

The RPD concluded that the appellants did not establish that the cartel was motivated to pursue them in the proposed IFA cities, namely, Mérida or Campeche, or that it had the ability to do so. I am of the view opinion that the RPD erred in its analysis of the evidence. The cartel's intention to locate the male appellant and his family

The RPD concluded that the fact that the cartel members [translation] "waited two years before showing up, attempting to grab the baby from the female claimant's hands on May 9, 2018,"2 does not establish that they would be motivated to locate them should they return to Mexico. The RPD stated the following at paragraph 17 of its decision: [Translation] 17. With respect to the criminals in question and their interest in finding him, the male claimant explained that it was out of a need to get rid of a witness who was a nuisance. However, given that the criminals waited two years to find him despite knowing where he lived, as alleged at the hearing, when the male claimant still lived in Acapulco, the city where the incident he witnessed occurred, the panel concludes, on a balance of probabilities, that the criminals in question did not demonstrate an interest in finding the male claimant to kill him or otherwise go after him.

First, the evidence reveals that the male appellant and his family lived in the city of Léon, in the state of Guanajuato, where the incidents occurred, not in Acapulco. According to their written account and their testimony, the appellants left their home on February 15, 2016, to seek refuge in a house that belonged to the female appellant's sister, an hour away from their home. According to them, they could not afford to move to another part of the country. Although the house was in the same city, there is no evidence on the record that their assailants knew this new location, as the RPD indicates. The evidence reveals only that the cartel members found them at this location two years later.

In addition, the fact that the cartel members pursued them two years after the events shows that they were motivated to do so and, at the very least, to intimidate them into withdrawing their police complaint. This is clear from the attempted abduction of the baby on May 9, 2018, when the female appellant was on her way to the pediatrician, and from the fact that their assailants went to their new residence, broke the windows and left a note indicating [translation] "I know where you live."

I am of the view that the passage of two years is not a determinative factor in assessing their assailants' interest in going after the appellants, should they return to Mexico. This does not, in my opinion, make it less likely that they would be motivated to intimidate or eliminate a potential witness. This is especially true in light of the documentary evidence indicating that Mexico has "extremely low rates of prosecution for all forms of crime," and prosecutions "could take years to complete."3

Furthermore, it is worth noting that the Jalisco cartel is extremely powerful and violent. The objective evidence indicates that, in "2015, the Mexican government declared CJNG one of the most dangerous cartels in the country and one of two with the most extensive reach.4" It also indicates "that making a complaint to a state authority against a gang would lead to pressure to drop the complaint and 'almost certainly' lead to death if the individual did not comply.5"

On the basis of this evidence and the incidents experienced by the male appellant, I conclude that it has been established that it is more likely than not that the agents of persecution are still interested in pursuing the appellants who filed a complaint against them. The cartel's ability to find the appellants in the internal flight alternative

As the appellants submit, I am of the opinion that the RPD did not take into account all of the documentary evidence with respect to the Jalisco cartel's ability to find the appellants should they return to Mérida or Campeche. Accordingly, the RPD's conclusion in this regard is erroneous.

The RPD had this to say at paragraph 16 of its decision: [Translation] In the panel's view, although the Jalisco cartel wields undeniable influence, the documentary evidence on Mexico reveals that its activities are limited to the central part of the country and that it operates in only 14 states in all. The cartel is not active in Mérida or in Yucatan, for example, states with some of the lowest crime rates in Mexico, according to the documentary evidence. On this basis, the panel concludes that the male claimant did not establish, on a balance of probabilities, the Jalisco cartel's ability to find him anywhere in Mexico. (emphasis added by the panel)

However, Tab 7.2 contains the following information regarding the presence and influence of Jalisco in Mexico: To best understand CJNG's international reach, it is important to first consider its expansion within Mexico. In 2016, many analysts maintained the cartel had presence throughout the country in a combined area that made up nearly half of Mexico. Recent reports indicate the group has pushed further into Aguas Calientes, San Luis Potosi, and Zacatecas states.... Despite leadership losses, Cartel Jalisco-New Generation has extended its geographic reach and maintained its own cohesion while exploiting the splintering of the Sinaloa organization. It is considered both a newer and extremely powerful cartel, based in Mexico's second-largest city of Guadalajara, and has a presence in 22 of 32 Mexican states.... Recently, some analysts have identified Cartel Jalisco-New Generation as a cartel with national reach.6 (emphasis added by the panel)

Even if the proposed IFA cities are outside Jalisco's area of operation, I agree with the appellants that the objective evidence establishes that the Jalisco cartel has the ability to find its victims anywhere in the country.

The evidence states that "a large debt or a personal vendetta could motivate a gang to track someone outside their area, and that gangs can use 'corrupt law enforcement agents' to obtain information about people they pursue."7 The evidence also establishes that "in order to extend their influence beyond their areas of operation, cartels rely on the 'representation' they have in other areas."

It specifically notes that Jalisco has "developed 'strategic alliances' with groups in other regions, including Los Zetas and Gulf Cartel splinter groups along the Gulf Coast."8 According to the "Stratfor Cartel Map by region of Influence (2018)," the Tamaulipas, Los Zetas remnants and Gulf Cartel remnants groups are present and have influence in the Yucatán Peninsula, where the two proposed IFA cities are located.9 Moreover, this map shows that all of Mexico is under the influence of cartels.

Accordingly, it is my opinion that the documentary evidence establishes that the Jalisco cartel has the ability and resources to locate the appellants in Mérida or Campeche, owing to its alliances with Los Zetas and Cartel del Golfo. Therefore, the RPD erred on this point. As previously explained, Jalisco also has the ability to locate the appellants in another part of Mexico through its alliances with other cartels that are present throughout the country. In my opinion, even though the principal appellant was the only one who witnessed the crime committed by the Jalisco members, the death threats and acts of intimidation were directed against the entire family.

Consequently, I conclude that it has been established, on a balance of probabilities, that all the appellants would be subjected to a risk to their lives or to unusual treatment or punishment should they return to Mexico. State protection

The objective evidence shows that the state does not have the power to protect victims pursued by the cartels, which are often more powerful than the public authorities. Sources note that organized crime organizations "seek to dominate and intimidate local politicians" and "control local administration budgets" or "infiltrate[e] local governments and law enforcement.10" Local newspapers report cases of police officers being shot after attending to families who were threatened by criminals.11

There is also evidence of the corruption of state officials and the fact that police forces at times collude with criminal groups.12 As previously mentioned, the prosecution rate for all forms of crime is extremely low and prosecutions can take years to complete.13 The witness protection program lacks financial resources and has a number of flawed protection measures.14

I am of the opinion that this evidence rebuts the presumption that adequate state protection is available to victims pursued by cartel members. In this case, the male appellant witnessed a crime committed by members of the Jalisco cartel and threats against him and his family that he reported to police. The evidence establishes that the cartel members repeatedly threatened the male appellant's family so that he would withdraw his complaint. Despite that, police did nothing to protect the male appellant and his family. Accordingly, I conclude that adequate protection from the Jalisco cartel would not be available to the appellants should they return to Mexico.

Under paragraph 111(1)(b) of the IRPA, I set aside the RPD's determination and substitute a determination that, in my opinion, should have been made, and I find that the appellants, XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, his spouse, XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, and their minor children, XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX and XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, are persons in need of protection under section 97 of the IRPA.

The appeal is allowed. (Signed) Bianca Eleonora Suciu Me Bianca Eleonora Suciu December 4, 2019 Date IRB translation Original language: French 1 Rozas del Solar v.
